799.title: Seven steps behind Death
799.hook: Savitri walks behind Yama, talking about the good, and Death keeps stopping to listen
799.carry: satsang: the company of the good
799.howItsDone: In the epic, each gift Yama offers Savitri on the road follows a speech of hers about dharma and the company of the good; Hindus call time spent near the good satsang.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-NINETY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yama, the lord of death, with Satyavan's life in his noose, and Savitri getting up to follow. Your line was the body dies; the self is not slain.
screen: `SAVITRI AND SATYAVAN.` · `SHE FOLLOWS DEATH.`

segments.voice: Yama hears footsteps behind him. He is heading south with Satyavan's life bound in his noose, and someone is following. He turns. Go back, Savitri, he tells her. Go and perform his last rites. You have come as far as anyone can come. She doesn't argue about the distance. She talks about something else entirely. And Death stops to listen. Behind them, in the clearing, Satyavan's body lies still under the trees.
screen: `FOOTSTEPS BEHIND DEATH.` → `GO BACK, SAVITRI.` → `DEATH STOPS TO LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Savitri's first answer is simple. Where my husband is taken, I go too. Then she speaks of friendship. The wise say, she tells him, that seven steps walked together with the good make a friendship. We have walked more than that, you and I. So, as a friend, hear me. Those seven steps aren't just a figure of speech. At a Hindu wedding the couple take seven steps together, the saptapadi, and with them become friends for life. Yama is pleased. Ask a gift, he says, anything except his life. Savitri asks that her blind father-in-law may see. Granted. Now go back, you're worn out. How could I be tired, she answers, walking beside my husband? And she keeps talking: even one meeting with the good bears fruit, she says, and time with them is never wasted. Another gift. Give my father-in-law back his kingdom. Granted. She speaks of how the good are kind even to those who wrong them. A third gift: sons for her own father. Every gift for someone else. Here is the teaching under the road. Hindus have a word for what Savitri is praising: satsang. Sat, the good and true; sang, company. Being near the good changes you. It's why families gather at the mandir or at home to sing bhajans and hear stories like this one. And look who it changes here. Not Savitri. Death himself keeps stopping to listen. She hasn't asked for Satyavan once. Not yet.
screen: `WHERE HE GOES, I GO.` · `SEVEN STEPS MAKE A FRIEND.` · `SIGHT, THEN A KINGDOM, THEN SONS.` · then, large: `SATSANG: THE COMPANY OF THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Take seven slow steps if you have room, or seven slow breaths where you are. With each one, bring to mind someone good you've walked beside: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend. Let one good thing about them come forward, and decide when you'll next sit in their company. If you pray, or know a bhajan, let it hold them; if not, simply be glad of them.
Sat, the good, the true, and the first half of satsang, the company of the good. Savitri walks behind Death, talking about the good, and asking every gift for someone else. Today's word.
screen: `SAT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: satsang, the company of the good. Seven steps, and Death became a listener. That's day seven hundred ninety-nine.

screen: `DAY 799 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BOON BEYOND COMPARE.`

800.title: The boon beyond compare
800.hook: the last gift, Satyavan's life given back, and why women still wind thread round a banyan
800.carry: a vrat offers your fast for another's long life
800.howItsDone: Markandeya ends the story by turning back to Yudhishthira's question about Draupadi. Outside the epic, many married women keep Vat Savitri in Jyeshtha: a fast, worship of a banyan, thread wound round it, and the story told aloud.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: sat, the good, and satsang, the company of the good. Three gifts from Death, sight, a kingdom and sons, and every one for someone else. Your line was satsang, the company of the good.
screen: `SAT AND SATSANG.` · `THREE GIFTS, ALL GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Ask once more, says Death. Savitri is still on the road behind Yama, still talking. And this time she asks for something for herself. Let me have sons, she says, sons of my own, born of Satyavan. Yama grants it. So be it. She keeps walking, and keeps speaking about the good. A gift has now been given that can only come true one way. And the noose in Yama's hand is still closed.
screen: `ASK ONCE MORE.` → `SONS, BORN OF SATYAVAN.` → `THE NOOSE STILL CLOSED.`

segments.voice: In the epic this isn't a clever trap. It's a conversation won. Savitri speaks again about the good, how they keep to the truth and hold up the world, and Yama, pleased once more, tells her to ask for something beyond compare. Savitri asks plainly. The gift you gave me can't come true without my husband. Without him I don't want happiness, or heaven, or my own life. Let Satyavan live. And Yama loosens the noose. Satyavan opens his eyes in her lap like a man waking from a long sleep. It's night, he's weak and frightened for his parents, so Savitri ties up her hair, helps him up, carries his axe, and they walk home through the dark. The sage Markandeya, who tells this story to the exiled Pandavas, promises them that Draupadi will save them the same way. Now the teaching. Every year, in the month of Jyeshtha, many married Hindu women keep Vat Savitri. They fast, worship a banyan tree, wind thread around it, and tell this story aloud. In popular tellings Satyavan lay under a banyan, a tree that lives for centuries, so it stands for the long life Savitri won. A vrat like this is one of Hinduism's oldest ways to love someone: you give something up yourself, often food, and offer it for another person's long life. Savitri began with a three-night fast before her husband's last day, and finished with her words on the road.
screen: `A CONVERSATION WON, NOT A TRAP.` · `LET SATYAVAN LIVE.` · `VAT SAVITRI, UNDER THE BANYAN.` · then, large: `A VRAT FOR ANOTHER'S LONG LIFE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose long life you wish for, someone you can still call or sit beside, and let their face come clear. If someone you've lost comes to mind instead, hold them kindly too.

801.title: The deer and the fire-sticks
801.hook: a deer runs off with a brahmin's fire-sticks, the Pandavas chase it to save his sacred fire, and a voice at a lake says: answer first
801.carry: agni carries the offering to the gods
801.howItsDone: The Yaksha's questions are a dialogue on dharma set in the Pandavas' forest years, and the episode opens with the brothers' chase to recover a brahmin's arani, the fire-sticks for his sacred fire.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: vara, a boon. Savitri talked with Death until he gave Satyavan back, and women still keep Vat Savitri for her. Your line was a vrat offers your fast for another's long life.
screen: `VARA, A BOON FROM DEATH.` · `A VRAT FOR ANOTHER'S LIFE.`

segments.voice: A pair of fire-sticks, swinging from a deer's antlers. A brahmin comes running to the Pandavas in their forest exile. He had left his arani, the two pieces of wood he rubs together to kindle his sacred fire, hanging on a tree. A deer rubbed against the tree, the sticks caught in its antlers, and now it's bounding away with them. Without them, he can't keep his fire. The five brothers take up their bows and go after it, deeper into the trees than any of them meant to go.
screen: `FIRE-STICKS ON A DEER'S ANTLERS.` → `A BRAHMIN'S FIRE AT STAKE.` → `FIVE BROTHERS GIVE CHASE.`

segments.voice: Why would five princes risk their lives for two sticks of wood? Because of what the sticks make. In the Vedas, Agni, the god of fire, is the messenger who carries offerings up to the gods. A Vedic householder kept a sacred fire, and kindled it by rubbing the arani together. Without them, the brahmin can't kindle his sacred fire, his line to the gods. Protecting it is a king's dharma, so the brothers run. And that fire is still at the center of Hindu life. At a wedding the couple walk around a fire, with Agni as their witness. When a family moves into a new home, a priest often lights a havan in the living room. But the deer stays just out of reach. They shoot and miss, and it's gone. Parched, they sink down under a tree, and Yudhishthira sends Nakula to climb it and look for water. Nakula sees green plants and cranes, and goes alone. He finds a lake, clear and still. He is about to drink when a voice speaks from nowhere. Don't be rash, child. This lake is mine. Answer my questions first, then drink. Nakula is burning with thirst. He kneels, drinks, and falls down dead on the bank. The questions haven't been asked yet.
screen: `AGNI, MESSENGER TO THE GODS.` · `FIRE AT THE HEART OF HINDU LIFE.` · `THE DEER ESCAPES. NAKULA SEEKS WATER.` · then, large: `HE DRINKS, AND FALLS.`

segments.voice: If you have a diya or a candle, light it and set it where you can see it; if not, picture one. Watch the flame for a few breaths. Many Hindu homes light a lamp like this every morning or evening. Think of one thing you'd like to offer today: a kind word, an hour of work, a meal shared. If you pray, offer it into the flame in your own words; if not, simply set your intention by the light.
Arani, the fire-sticks that kindle a sacred fire, carried off on a deer's antlers. Five brothers chase them for a brahmin's fire, and one brother drinks before he listens. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: agni carries the offering to the gods. Two sticks of wood, and five brothers ran for them. Until tomorrow.

802.title: Four brothers at the lake
802.hook: one by one the brothers take from the yaksha's lake without asking, and why Hindus ask the earth's pardon each morning
802.carry: ask the earth's leave before you take
802.howItsDone: In the epic, the four brothers fall one by one before Yudhishthira arrives, each warned by the same voice in the same words. Many Hindus touch the floor on waking and ask Mother Earth's pardon, and a bhoomi puja asks her leave before building.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: arani, the brahmin's fire-sticks, kept for Agni, and Nakula, who drank before he listened. Your line was agni carries the offering to the gods.
screen: `ARANI, KEPT FOR AGNI.` · `NAKULA DRANK, AND FELL.`

segments.voice: Nakula doesn't come back. Under the tree, his brothers wait, and wait, and Yudhishthira sends the next one. Sahadeva, go and find your brother, and bring water. So Sahadeva follows the cranes to the lake, and there is Nakula, lying on the bank. Sahadeva is grieving, and burning with thirst, and the voice speaks again, the same words. This lake is mine. Answer first. Back under the tree, three brothers are still waiting for water.
screen: `NAKULA DOESN'T COME BACK.` → `SAHADEVA GOES NEXT.` → `THE SAME VOICE, THE SAME WORDS.`

segments.voice: Sahadeva drinks, and falls beside his brother. Now Yudhishthira sends Arjuna, the great archer. Arjuna sees both twins dead and looks for an enemy. When the voice speaks, he shoots at it by ear alone. The voice answers, unhurt: your arrows can't touch me. Answer my questions, and then drink. Arjuna drinks, and falls. Then Bhima comes, the strong one, sure this is some spirit's work and ready to fight it, after a drink. The voice warns him too. He drinks, and falls. Thirst, grief, aim and strength, and not one of them asks. Listen again to what the voice said first: this lake is mine. In Hindu tradition the world is full of owners you can't see. Rivers are goddesses. Yakshas guard lakes and trees. The earth herself is Bhumi Devi, Mother Earth. So many Hindus begin the day with a short verse to her before their feet touch the floor, asking her to forgive them for stepping on her. Before a house is built, a bhoomi puja asks her leave. One way to hear the lake, then: the brothers didn't fail for lack of strength. They took without asking the owner. Four heroes of the Mahabharata lie on the shore. One brother is left.
screen: `SAHADEVA FALLS. ARJUNA SHOOTS.` · `NOT ONE OF THEM ASKS.` · `BHUMI DEVI, MOTHER EARTH.` · then, large: `THEY TOOK WITHOUT ASKING.`

segments.voice: Before you stand up from this, rest your fingertips on the floor, the way many Hindus do each morning. Feel the ground holding you up, as it has all day without being asked. Breathe in, and think of one thing you'll take from the earth today: water, food, a place to walk. If you pray, ask Bhumi Devi's pardon and thank her in your own words; if not, simply thank the ground, then touch your fingers to your heart.
Yaksha, the unseen spirit who owns the lake and asks before anyone may drink. Four brothers bring thirst, grief, aim and strength, and none of them asks the owner. Today's word.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the yaksha, the unseen owner of the lake, and four brothers who took the water without asking. Your line was ask the earth's leave before you take.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS.` · `FOUR BROTHERS ON THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: The last brother comes alone. Yudhishthira has waited under the tree as long as he can, and now he follows the cranes himself. He finds the lake, and all four of his brothers lying beside it. He weeps over each of them by name, and remembers what each one was to him. And then, through his grief, he does something none of them did. He looks. Before he touches the water, he reads the shore.
screen: `THE LAST BROTHER COMES ALONE.` → `HE WEEPS OVER EACH ONE.` → `THEN HE LOOKS.`

segments.voice: What Yudhishthira sees doesn't add up. No wounds on his brothers. No footprints of an enemy. Their faces haven't changed color, so he doesn't think it's poison. He steps down into the water, and the voice comes. I am a crane, it says. I killed your brothers. Answer my questions, or you'll be the fifth. No bird could do this, Yudhishthira says. Who are you? And he sees a yaksha, a huge spirit, speaking from up in a tree. Yudhishthira doesn't shoot, or fight, or drink. I don't want what's yours, he says. Ask, and I'll answer as well as I'm able. The questions begin. What is heavier than the earth? A mother. What is higher than the sky? A father. What is faster than the wind? The mind. What is more numerous than blades of grass? Our thoughts. The yaksha asks about the size of the world, and Yudhishthira answers with a family. This is one of Hinduism's oldest teachings. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends his students home with these words: let your mother be a god to you, let your father be a god to you. It's why Hindu children bow and touch the feet of their parents and elders, and get a hand on the head and a blessing back. Not because elders are always right. Because what they carried for you weighs more than the earth.

If you pray, bring them into your prayer.

804.title: Four friends for four seasons
804.hook: riddles about fish and rivers, then four friends for four seasons, and the last friend is what you gave
804.carry: dana: what you give goes with you
804.howItsDone: The middle of the Yaksha's questions mixes riddles about fish and rivers with plain guidance: the friend of the dying is charity, dana, and pride, anger, desire and greed are worth giving up.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the yaksha-prashna began. Heavier than the earth, a mother; higher than the sky, a father. Your line was honor parents, heavier than earth, higher than sky.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS.` · `HEAVIER THAN THE EARTH? A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: What sleeps with its eyes open? The yaksha keeps going, and some of the questions are pure fun. A fish, Yudhishthira answers. What doesn't move once it's born? An egg. What has no heart? A stone. What grows by its own force? A river. Four brothers lie dead on the shore, and the talk sounds almost like a game by a campfire. Then the questions turn toward people.
screen: `WHAT SLEEPS WITH ITS EYES OPEN?` → `A FISH, AN EGG, A STONE, A RIVER.` → `THEN, WHO STANDS BY US?`

segments.voice: Who is the friend of a traveler far from home? A companion on the road, Yudhishthira answers. The friend of someone who keeps a home? The wife. Of someone who is sick? The physician. And of someone about to die? Charity, the gifts they've given. Four friends for four seasons of a life. Remember who is answering: a man in exile, whose companions on the road lie dead behind him. Hold on to that last friend, because it's a big Hindu teaching. Hindus call it dana, giving. Wealth stays behind when you die; what you gave goes with you, as your karma. It's why giving runs through Hindu life: food at the temple, money in the hundi, gifts at a birth or a wedding, and in the name of loved ones who have died. Then the yaksha asks about letting go. What, given up, makes you agreeable? Pride. What leaves no regret? Anger. What makes you rich, once you let it go? Desire. And what makes you happy, once it's gone? Greed. Hindu teachers count six inner enemies: desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy. Four of them are right here at the lake. Notice they fit together. Greed holds on; dana lets go. The answers come out plain and small, from a man whose brothers' lives depend on them.
screen: `A COMPANION FOR THE TRAVELER.` · `A HEALER FOR THE SICK.` · `CHARITY FOR THE DYING.` · then, large: `DANA: WHAT YOU GIVE GOES WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind, one at a time, the friends of your own seasons: someone who was a companion when you were far from home, someone who shares your home, someone who looked after you when you were sick. Let each face stay for a few breaths, and thank them silently. Then choose one small gift to give today, food, time or money, given quietly. If you pray, you can offer it in your prayer.
Mitra, a friend, is what the yaksha asks about: for a traveler, a householder, the sick and the dying. Four friends for four seasons, and the last one is dana, what you gave. Today's word.
screen: `MITRA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: dana, what you give goes with you. Four friends for four seasons, and the last one is what you gave away. That's day eight hundred four.

805.title: Hidden in a cave
805.hook: four big questions, and the answer Hindus still use when the texts disagree: walk where the great have walked
805.carry: dharma is hidden; walk where the great walked
805.howItsDone: On the path, Yudhishthira concedes that argument is unsettled and the scriptures differ, and points to the way the great have gone; Hindu law books likewise count the conduct of good people as a source of dharma.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: mitra, a friend. A companion for the traveler, a healer for the sick, and for the dying, dana, what they gave. Your line was dana, what you give goes with you.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS.` · `A FRIEND FOR EVERY SEASON.`

segments.voice: Four more questions, and they're the big ones. The yaksha has asked about the sun and the earth, about friends and anger and greed. Now he asks four in a row. Who is happy? What is wonderful? What is the path? And what is the news? Four brothers are still lying on the shore. The answers have to be true, not clever, and Yudhishthira gives each one in a sentence or two.
screen: `WHO IS HAPPY?` → `WHAT IS WONDERFUL?` → `WHAT IS THE PATH? WHAT IS THE NEWS?`

segments.voice: Who is happy? Yudhishthira's answer is wonderfully small. The person who cooks simple greens in their own home, late in the day, who owes nothing to anyone, and doesn't have to live away from home. Hear that from a prince in exile. What is the news? The world is a great cooking pot. Time is the cook, with the sun for fire and days and nights for fuel, stirring every creature with the months and seasons for a ladle. What is wonderful? Every day, living beings go to the house of Death, and those who are left live as if they never will. And what is the path? Here he's honest about how hard it is. Argument doesn't settle it. The scriptures say different things. There isn't one sage whose view everyone accepts. The truth of dharma is hidden as if in a cave. So the path is the one the great have walked. That answer is a big Hindu teaching. Hinduism has no single book or pope to settle every question. The old law books name the Vedas and tradition as sources of dharma, and beside them, the conduct of good people. So when the texts seem to disagree, Hindus look to how the wise and good actually live. The week began with Savitri talking with Death on the road. It ends with a brother talking with a stranger at a lake. In both, the one who speaks truly about dharma saves the others.
screen: `HAPPY: GREENS AT HOME, AND NO DEBTS.` · `THE NEWS: TIME COOKS EVERY CREATURE.` · `THE WONDER: WE LIVE AS IF WE WON'T DIE.` · then, large: `THE PATH: WHERE THE GREAT HAVE WALKED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose life shows you dharma: a grandparent, a teacher, someone quietly good. Let their face come clear. Now think of one choice in front of you this week, and ask, without arguing it out, what would they do? Breathe with that answer for a few breaths. If you pray, ask for the courage to walk where they walked.

Dharma, the right way, hidden as if in a cave, Yudhishthira says, so we follow the path the great have walked. Supper at home, time stirring the pot, and the wonder that we live as if we never die. Today's word.
screen: `DHARMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: dharma is hidden; walk where the great walked. Greens, a home, and a path someone good has already worn. Until tomorrow.
